title: Norm-Formation Laboratory
summary: Fifteen rounds of a deliberately unanchored judgement: five made alone, five with three simulated others' estimates visible, and five alone again. The three others are generated from anchors drawn around the learner's own opening mean, so the emerging norm is not imposed from outside; the learner's own convergence is never forced or modelled. A final comparison shows three other simulated groups arriving at quite different norms from the identical display, and the historical experiment whose logic the activity borrows is described separately with its criticisms.
learningObjectives: Describe what happens to an unanchored judgement when other people's judgements become visible.
Explain why a frame that persists once the group has gone cannot be explained as compliance.
Account for why different groups reach different norms from the same display.
Distinguish agreeing with an explicit demand from acquiring a shared definition of the situation.
State the boundary conditions on the finding, including the role of ambiguity.
topics: history and criticism of a classic study
interactionTypes: trace chart with full text equivalent
privacy: Estimates are used only to draw the chart in the browser tab and are discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person is produced.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed and nothing is scored; the task is entirely self-paced and a simulated-participant route runs all fifteen rounds for anyone who would rather not answer or is demonstrating from the front. The stimulus is deliberately uninformative and the sentence beneath it carries everything the drawing does, so a learner who cannot see it is at no disadvantage - the ambiguity is stipulated rather than perceptual, and the page says so. The trace chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence listing every estimate by phase with each phase mean; the group phase is marked by a shaded band and by a label inside it. The number input accepts Enter, validates its range and explains a rejected value rather than reporting an error. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Alone, together, alone again: how a shared frame of reference forms under ambiguity and outlives the group
simulationNotes: No autokinetic effect is involved and no materials, procedure or data from any historical experiment are reproduced; the display is a drawing with no scale, and the historical study is described separately on the page along with five criticisms. The three other participants are generated only after the learner's first five estimates, from anchors at 0.45, 0.85 and 1.75 times the learner's own opening mean, so the emerging norm is not imposed from outside. On each group round every simulated participant moves 42 per cent of the way towards the running group mean plus noise. The learner's own estimates are never modelled or constrained. The three comparison groups are four simulated participants each, drawn around openings of 0.35, 1.1 and 2.6 times the learner's opening mean and run through the identical rule; in a representative run they arrive at 3.6, 12.4 and 29.3 cm against the learner's group at 11.4 cm. All randomness comes from a mulberry32 generator seeded at 20260214, reseeded on reset. That the demonstration converges is a property of the model; the evidence that people converge is in the literature, not on the page.
